utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. We are told there are a number -- or there is at least one matter, there may be more, that counsel wish to raise before we continue. Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to inform the Trial Chamber about a disclosure error involving the witness who is currently testifying which I discovered last evening. You'll recall yesterday during the witness's testimony that the witness mentioned that he had conversations with an OTP investigator in which he told -- including at least one face-to-face meeting, in which he told the investigator that portions of his statement from 2004 to the ICTY were either not correct or not -- not true. Following that testimony, I directed my staff via e-mail yesterday to search for any such information, and the Prosecution team yesterday afternoon located information which confirms what the witness said, at least vis-a-vis a face-to-face meeting that took place in February of this year in Skopje, and that -- this information was recorded on what is called a witness information form, which is usually information that is only shared between the Office of the Prosecutor and the Victims and Witness Unit, which is part of the reason why I did not discover this information earlier. And the information that was recorded by the investigator states that during this conversation with the witness in February of this year to confirm that the witness would be a witness for the Prosecution, the witness told the investigator that much of what was in his 2004 statement was either not true or incorrect and explained some of the reasons for that. When I discovered that we had this information last night which we had not disclosed previously to the Defence, I immediately ran down to the Defence counsel room and gave a copy to Ms. Residovic; and then subsequently, I e-mailed a copy to counsel for Mr. Tarculovski so they have this information, in case they wish to use it during cross-examination. This was my mistake, Your Honour. The investigator who recorded this information attempted to bring it to my attention via e-mail on the 2nd of March this year but apparently, I was distracted and it slipped through the cracks. So this was my error and the Prosecution apologises for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Saxon. You have informed counsel and we are still in the process of dealing with the witness. Thank you. Is there any matter that needs to be dealt with at this stage, any other matter? Yes, indeed, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. Simply to express our gratitude first to Mr. Saxon for providing the statement in question to us last night. We also sent a further request to Mr. Saxon to conduct a search for any similar material as might have pertained to past or future witnesses. There are two other matters, perhaps, which could be raised at this stage, if the Chamber is minded to do so. The first one relates to the timing of the return of one of the Prosecution witness, Mr. Hutsch. We have had some exchange of e-mail with Mr. Saxon, and I understand that Mr. Saxon has sought to obtain some information in that regard, the Defence would be very keen to obtain clear guidance and information as to the time of the return of Mr. Hutsch. We had understood from Your Honours's statement and instructions before the break that this witness should come during the last two weeks of the month of August and it seems to be, at this stage, quite compromised, if we understand the information we've received from the Prosecution. The next matter which we would like to query at this stage and again if the Chamber is minded to seek information from the Prosecution is the length, or the foreseen length of the remainder of the case and also further witnesses dropped from the Prosecution case. At this stage, we can indicate that the Prosecution kindly informed the Defence yesterday that at least one witness who appears on this list will probably or most likely not be called by the Prosecution. Finally, I will simply indicate that there's a number of issues which we still discuss with the Prosecution, in particular, in relation to further disclosure of material and we hope at this stage to be able to sort it out directly with the Prosecution. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mettraux. Anything further? Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, prior to the summer recess, the Prosecution via the Victim Witness Section, tried to communicate with Mr. Hutsch to obtain his presence here during the last two weeks of this month. The information that the Prosecution received back through VWS was that if Mr. Hutsch came here at the end of this month, he would only be able to do that for two days, because of his other professional commitments. And that he would not commit to the four-day period that he is required to come back for until the 15th of -- excuse me, the information that was received from VWS was that Mr. Hutsch would not commit to the four days that are necessary to complete his testimony until the end of October. When I received that information, I spoke with members of VWS and asked them to please get back in touch with Mr. Hutsch and ask him to commit to the four-day period beginning on the 15th of October, Monday, the 15th, I believe, through Thursday the 18th. VWS has sent e-mails, has left telephone messages. We do not have a response yet from Mr. Hutsch. I did not want to agree to bringing Mr. Hutsch back again only for two days because then I felt we would have the same problem, because the Defence has told us they need three more days for cross-examination and I did not want to create another situation where cross-examination was going to be interrupted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In short, you don't know at the moment when it would be convenient to have the witness back.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I cannot confirm at the moment. I'm hoping it will be Monday, the 15th of October, but we are waiting for confirmation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: With respect to the other matter, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The length of the Prosecution's case, I've done some calculations. First of all, it is correct what Mr. Mettraux said, the Prosecution does intend to drop one more witness from its witness list and we will inform the Chamber of that in writing in the near future. With that reduction, if the witness testimony proceeds at the pace that was going prior to the summer recess, according to the estimates that I made in the Prosecution's filing of the 12th of July, there would still be approximately 11 more weeks of Prosecution evidence remaining, which would take us into the first week of November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, in forming that estimate, on what basis have you allowed time for cross-examination, Mr. Saxon?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I have kept to the conservative estimates that the Prosecution submitted in its revised calculations to the Chamber on the 12th of July. In other words, I'm continuing to follow the same estimates, the same extended number of hours permitted for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It was the experience of the Chamber that in the weeks until the break we were not maintaining that rate of progress. Is that something that you have not made any allowance for?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I did not make allowance for that, Your Honour. I did not. Having said -- this week, Your Honour, according to the Defence, we will actually be under that estimate. So I decided --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What alarms me in particular was to see an estimate for a witness next week where some nearly 12 hours of cross-examination was being proposed for one relatively routine witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, there have been communications between the Prosecution and Defence counsel quite recently where the Prosecution has asked Defence counsel to inform the Prosecution whether Defence counsel believe they will use less time for cross-examination than estimated by the Prosecution, and the only estimate that we have received where the time would be less would be for the current witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber would indicate that its concern with the slow rate of progress is reaching the point where contrary to its preference to leave it to counsel to be mindful of the need for considerable economy of time that the point is virtually now reached when it will be necessary for the Chamber to impose time-limits to try and bring the total length of this trial within some reasonable limit. I make that very clear now, because in the next two weeks, if there is not a clear indication from the actual progress made, that the matter of time is under control with each witness, counsel will have to expect that time-limits will be imposed. So we're really allowing just two weeks more, this week and next week, to see whether there can be a considerable discipline imposed about time; and if that cannot be, we will have to take the step of imposing some arbitrary limits, in the interests of trying to ensure that this case finishes within a more reasonable time. I hope that indication is clear enough to counsel, and we will watch progress closely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't think it's a time when we can expect Defence counsel to make any useful observation or submission about the matter of progress, and in view of that, we will just move now to continue the evidence of the witness but ask counsel to take very careful note of what has just been said. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Could I remind you that the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence still applies and we apologise that you were kept waiting as we dealt with some other matters. Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Jakovoski.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, in answering my questions, you said that you, together with Mr. Boskoski, came to Ljubanci and that as you recalled a policeman, an Albanian, led you to the place where you came out of the vehicle. Do you recall talking about this yesterday?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You then said at 3938 page of the transcript, you said that you remember of a head of a municipality with whom the minister then spoke with. Once again, you met this head on page 3940 of the transcript, and 3941, line 19. I would ask you to clarify what you said. You said that this was the head of this municipality where you were at. If I were to try to recall to you that the municipality of this place is the municipality of Cair in the city of Skopje, would this lead you to remember that this was in fact the municipality of Cair?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it was the municipality of Cair. That is where the village is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you said that the head of this municipality was there, was I correct in understanding that you wanted to say that, in effect, this was the head of the unit of internal affairs of this municipality, that is to say, the police of the municipality of Cair, and not the mayor. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, the person with whom the Minister Boskoski met and with whom he spoke with and who explained to the minister various issues and things was the head of the police of the municipality of Cair; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you did not speak of the name of the head of this municipality. I would ask that the witness be now shown 65 ter 1D497, page 1D4519. It is only in the English language, and this is the segment of the statement of Branko Pejcinovski. In this point, it is stated: [In English] When we arrived there, there are a lot of person just when we stepped out, the minister and met the other commander, Ljube Krstevski. I can't say that was the conversation about." [Interpretation] Is this statement of Branko Pejcinovski, can this lead you to remember that this head of the police of the municipality of Cair is, in effect, Ljube Krstevski, the head of OVR Cair?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I agree that it was Krstevski, the person whom the minister spoke to at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is, in fact, the person who, for the whole time of your sojourn in and stay in the courtyard in the house where you entered was in the vicinity of the minister and he was the only person whom you remembered explaining anything to the minister. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If I were to put to you that it was evident upon leaving and upon your arrival there that the minister did know what was going on and that Ljube Krstevski explained something to me, would this be correct to say?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My apology if the question was complex. I want to ask you the following: Is your view of the situation in which you found yourself in was such that you, at that moment, concluded that, in effect, the Minister Boskoski, prior to arriving to this place did not know what was going on there? Is this conclusion that I am making correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Seems to the Prosecution that the witness is being asked to speculate as to the knowledge of the accused Boskoski at that time. We don't know whether the witness can do that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreters wish to point that the witness answered that question but we could not give the answer because the Prosecutor spoke at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The concern of Mr. Saxon, Ms. Residovic, is that you are asking the witness to conjecture. Is there anything you want to say about that?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm asking only about what the experience of the witness was at that time, not what the minister knew at that time. I asked whether the witness could have concluded and the minister did not know what was going on. The witness responded to this. However, if you feel that the question is to be rephrased --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now we have not recorded it. We have not -- the answer was not able to be identified because it was overtaken, and I'm still struggling with your proposition.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you please tell me when you went towards Ljubanci, did you personally know what was going on there?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did the minister perhaps, during the drive, tell you that he knows what's going on there?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't know either.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And when you arrived there, when the head Krstevski explained to him, was it evident that this was -- the minister was receiving first information about what was going on there?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You personally had not been there prior to that day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And not alone, not with the minister, you had not been there prior, to Ljubanci?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have never been there before.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And to the question of the Prosecution, you said that you did not pay attention to the content of the conversation between the head and the minister because it was customary that your care was to care of the safety of the minister. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also stated when you stopped you heard shots in the village. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, the Prosecution showed you a video-clip where you recognised yourself and you recognised also the minister. Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Prior to that, to the question of the Prosecution you confirmed that there you found a large number of people but you said that you were not sure of their number. You said it could have been 20 or hundred and this is noted in the transcript on page 3938 to 3922 to 23 [as interpreted]. Is this what you said? Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember having said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: 65 ter 1D498, page 1D4527 in the English version, and 1D4541 -- 4541 D, item 17 in the Macedonian version. Do you see item 17? [In English] When we arrived, I have seen some army reservists and police reservists. One of them army reservist approached the minister and was crying because his best friend was killed. I don't know the details. I think this reservist was really disturbed, his colleagues took him away. At the arrival, I saw two people in civilian." [Interpretation] Tell me please, is it correct that in addition to the police reservists, you also saw there a number of army reservists?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And that you saw civilians. Is this also correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were many civilians there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, as you said, about the number, when asked by the Prosecution, you also cannot be sure of their number, the number of army reservists and civilians. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I could not say this precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would now ask that you be shown document 1D497, page 1D4519, item 27, 28, and 29. This is the statement of Branko Pejcinovski, again the deputy head of the security of which we talked about yesterday. He as we could see previously, that when you came there were a lot of people there, in item 26 this is said. However, in item 27 he says the following: [In English] I am sure that the minister spoke in front of garden also with villagers and calmed them down not to go in the village of Ljuboten. It was a lot of person. They were in civilian clothes, these men and women [indiscernible]. I think I have seen at this time hundred or more villagers." [Interpretation] My question to you, in view of this statement made by Branko Pejcinovski and your previous statement that you had seen only two civilians, could it be correct that you saw civilians but that you cannot at this point and at this moment say the exact number of civilians was there due to the same reasons that you cannot recall of other events as well?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you. Only I can't give you the exact number of the civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My learned colleague of the Prosecution showed you a video-clip yesterday, as I already said, where you recognised yourself and the minister. Due to this transcript this is evidence P363 MFI, and if you recall, on that clip you were standing next to a wall. Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And on that clip, you could see, and I'm asking you whether you recall, that the courtyard of the house was surrounded by a rather high wall?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And in that courtyard you could not see any kind of other fortifications or sandbags or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This wall was the only protection. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And if you recall of the video-clip which you saw yesterday, is it correct that it could -- that on a number of occasion it could be seen that there was shooting, that shooting could be heard and that people were protecting themselves behind the wall? Do you remember seeing this on the clip?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember since I was there, and this was shooting coming from the village towards the house.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And this was the reason why perhaps you and other persons who were there tried to take cover behind the wall, because the shooting was coming from the village towards your position. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And generally speaking, in view of the fact that with the minister you sometimes you were present in the battle grounds, is it correct to say that the walls of the houses were often used as protection?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When the Prosecution showed you the video-clip from the village of Matejce, we could see there the minister and that he had a helmet on his head. Do you recall this?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And to my question you responded that very often you asked of the minister to put on protective wear when you were close to places where there was shooting going on?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This time when you were in Ljubanci in this house, the minister was in civil wear?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: He did not have a helmet on his head. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You did not suggest this to you because you did not expect that you would find some kind of battle there. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And when you heard the shooting, as a body-guard, you were in a greater stress -- state of stress because of the safety of the minister. Could I phrase it in this way?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me please, through the wall which we saw as we saw on the video-clip, you looked on towards the village, could you see a lot? Was there a lot to be seen?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could not see anything above that wall. We could not see the village. We could not see any battle going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, when you saw - and this can be seen on the clip - did you see that there were only a few houses from which smoke could be seen? If you do not recall, this is not important. We saw the clip yesterday.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not remember now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Also, to the question of my learned colleague from the Prosecution, you said that in the courtyard of this house you remained about one and a half hours. This would also be an assessment of the situation -- which you can give of the situation today. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you were in the courtyard of that house, you did not at any point of time notice that Ljube Boskoski gave any kind of orders, whether to Ljube Krstevski or to someone else?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jakovoski, yesterday you stated before this Court that there were many occasions when you spoke to the OTP, actually the investigator of the OTP over the phone, and also you had a meeting with the investigator personally in a hotel in Skopje. On transcript page 3967, lines 9 to 11, you stated that there were at least five or six occasions when you spoke on the phone, and that for you that was some kind of a psychological problem. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: We received the notes of the investigator, and the investigator says that since 2004, until February of 2007, he phoned you 15 times. You can confirm that this could be true, but you do not remember the exact number?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall, but it could have been 15.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you stated that this posed a certain psychological problem to you, could I infer from this that you felt under pressure regarding your testimony?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, great.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will ask you now to -- to reply to certain personal questions and if you feel that you should not respond, I will not insist that you do. We spoke about your professional career development and your employment in police stations as a uniformed police officer. Tell me, please, is it correct that before coming to the security department you worked as an inspector in the department for illegal trafficking of drugs?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it also correct that you, after leaving the security of Mr. Boskoski, you again worked in the department for illegal trafficking of drugs as an inspector?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that there is a very difficult job and that you needed to work nights many times?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that in the Ministry of Interior for the sake of security of the inspectors themselves but also for protection to prevent them from abusing their office, there are tests carried out on the inspectors performing these duties in order to prevent any chance that some of the inspectors become drug abusers?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And very often you had passed those tests. You -- the tests were negative on you, and you never had any problems with drugs in your life; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Also, you never had any problems with alcohol.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So if anyone were to suggest that you could have had such problems, such suggestion would simply be incorrect. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you replied to the Prosecutor's question yesterday that you speak the truth today and that the change of power did not have any impact on you, is it correct that everything you said to the Prosecutor from the onset of the interviews was your personal wish to indicate to the Prosecutor that some of the things that you had previously stated were incorrect, that they were even false some of them?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And that decision of yours, your honesty in stating those facts to the Prosecutor were not caused by any pressure from someone; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This was not related also to the fact that the Albanians were not indicted before this Court. It was simply that you decided to speak the truth and that the Prosecutor should know that in time. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So if someone were to infer that you stated this due to some other reasons and not those that you confirmed now before this Court, that inference or that statement would be incorrect. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, I would like to ask you something else. You were asked yesterday by the Prosecutor about some allegedly private locations and then the restaurants, Del Fufo, Galija, and -- and another restaurant -- Dzino, yes, it's Dzino. Tell me, please, are the restaurants public locations?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And these restaurants Del Fufo, Galija and Dzino that were mentioned in the transcript, page 3926, lines 1 to 7, they are actually quite popular restaurants in Skopje and they're centrally located. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And they're frequented on a daily basis by many prominent personas. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But they are also frequented by ordinary citizens many of them regardless of their affiliation or national, political or any other provenance. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And practically, each of these restaurants is entered daily by many hundreds of people; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So what you have stated, these restaurants that the Prosecutor has mentioned are no private locations. They are public locations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And if I understood you well, the Minister Boskoski sometimes went privately to some of these restaurants; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: For you, the body-guards, it was actually always a problem when the minister would go to such places where there were tens or hundreds of people at each moment of time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Actually, this was again related to your fundamental duty, that you need to take care about the safety of the minister, and if I understood well, if I understood you well, many people would come and greet the minister; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct. Everybody wanted to extend greetings to the minister at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This would also happen when minister was walking down a street. People would come and greet him and that was always a stressful situation for you, the body-guards; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That was particularly stressful because that was the time of the crisis, and you never knew who could be someone -- who the person who comes to the minister is actually; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And I would like to ask you to tell me whether I understood you correctly, when you stated that maybe during some private outings, the minister met Bucuk, this could be understood as Bucuk, as simply anyone else coming to greet the minister. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But you could not confirm this fact with certainty; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you yourself couldn't confirm actually whether Bucuk was an acquaintance of the minister or not; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But what you can say with certainty is that you never saw him sitting with Bucuk or with Johan and having a conversation with them about something. This was something that you never saw yourself. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Your Honours, I have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Residovic. Mr. Apostolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. It is not because we were cautioned by the Court, but I will have no questions to ask of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's extremely speedy, Mr. Apostolski. Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Inspector, my colleague read to you some lines from a statement previously given to the Office of the Prosecutor by Mr. Branko Pejcinovski. And in particular, earlier this afternoon Ms. Residovic read you some lines from paragraph 30 of that statement with respect to the events at Ljubanci on the 12th of August and who Minister Boskoski spoke with there at that garden. And paragraph 30 begins like this: "Inside the garden" --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I did not cite, I did not quote item 30, rather, 27, 28 and 29. But I have also -- but I did quote the statement, so for the purpose of establishing correctness, I would like to say that I did not quote from this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm grateful for the correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You told my learned colleague that Minister Boskoski spoke to people in the garden and calmed them down, people at the garden and calmed them down. And then you mentioned that some people in the garden could have been civilians. Paragraph 30 of this witness statement begins like this: "Inside the garden he spoke with some civilians. There were also some individuals from the ministry in camouflage uniforms. I know them only by the face, no names." Yesterday you told us that when the minister entered that garden, police officers in uniform stood at attention; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I just want to clarify you, would those persons standing at attention have been the individuals from the ministry in camouflage uniforms in that garden mentioned by your colleague, Mr. Pejcinovski?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Earlier today my colleague asked you about telephone conversations and discussions that you had with an investigator from the Office of the Prosecutor, and you mentioned that the investigator may have called you around 15 times after you had already given your statement. Do you recall the investigator, during those telephone calls, asking to have a meeting with you, a face-to-face meeting with you?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he asked for such a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And do you recall that after the indictments against Mr. Boskoski and Mr. Tarculovski were released by this Tribunal, you refused to meet because you believed that the Tribunal was biased and unfair for not indicting ethnic Albanian suspects. Do you recall telling the investigator that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you recall telling the investigator during one telephone conversation that you now wanted to become the best witness for Brother Ljube, because The Hague Tribunal was not indicting Albanians. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not recall. This is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In 2001, did you know that the man known as Bucuk and other members of the Kometa security agency had a reputation for being criminals? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yesterday, Inspector, this is page 3956 of the transcript, you agreed with my colleague that in 2001, Mr. Boskoski's basic message was that you -- one should care for every human being and that all citizens, irrespective of their ethnic or religious affiliations, they should all be cared for, all those who love their country, Macedonia. Do you recall explaining that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In 2001, what was Minister Boskoski's attitude towards Macedonian citizens who criticised the actions of the security forces against the NLA?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the question? It is not quite clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did Minister Boskoski also feel that the rights of Macedonians who criticised the Macedonian security forces in their battle against the NLA should also be protected?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not competent to respond to this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did Minister Boskoski in 2001 ever refer to persons who criticised the security forces of Macedonia as traitors?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not say something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In 2001, did Minister Boskoski believe that -- I'll strike that. In 2001, did Minister Boskoski believe that more rights should be given to ethnic Albanians in Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, an objection. Already a number of questions that the Prosecution has asked are about the fact that -- or require the witness to express the views and the feelings of the minister, and just recently he objected to one of my similar questions in this respect. I don't think these are questions that should be put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: My inquiry began with comments made by the witness yesterday as to the "the basic message of Minister Boskoski." And what I would like to explore is what Minister Boskoski's message was about the rights of ethnic Albanians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And how does this arise in re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, what was said yesterday during cross-examination was that the Minister's basic message was "you should care for every human being and all citizens irrespective of their ethnic or religious affiliations, all those who love their country, Macedonia." This is at page 3956. So I would like to explore whether the minister's message also applied to ethnic Albanians seeking to expand their rights.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this segment, which my learned colleague is recalling is only a quotation. A part of the book which the Prosecutor had read himself, read at -- it fully but commented only on the first sentence where it is stated that the minister had worked day and night and at the end of this paragraph which was put in the direct examination was that Boskoski wrote in his book that this is a feeling he has towards all citizens of Macedonia, regardless of ethnic or religious affiliation. I don't think the Prosecution has the right to go back to what he had already himself asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The witness was asked to comment about this during cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Inspector, I'm going to ask my question again. During 2001 what was Minister Boskoski's message - to use the same word - regarding ethnic Albanians who sought to increase their rights in Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The very background and origin of the minister from the village of Celopek which is a mixed village, both Albanians and Macedonians lived together, and through there and through the Macedonia he fought for the equality of all citizens of Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did Minister Boskoski agree to the efforts of some ethnic Albanians to expand their constitutional rights in 2001?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, once again, I have to object, because this is not a question for this witness. He is a body-guard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be able to proceed, Ms. Residovic, on the same basis that earlier questioning has. Carry on, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Inspector, in 2001, did Minister Boskoski agree to the efforts of some ethnic Albanians in Macedonia to expand their constitutional rights.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpretation could not hear. Could the witness please repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You need to say that a bit more loudly.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: He did. The answer is yes. The answer is yes?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did he express his agreement to you?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to me personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So how do you know he agreed with this -- with these efforts by ethnic Albanians to increase their rights?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard through the television.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Yesterday at page 3959 of the transcript, you agreed with my learned colleague that in 2001 when Minister Boskoski received news that a police officer had been wounded or killed that he would take it very personally. Do you recall saying that, or agreeing with that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And at the same page in the transcript you agreed with my colleague that Minister Boskoski would always say that the police should not react in the same manner and that Minister Boskoski was not a person who sought revenge. Do you recall agreeing with that statement?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct. I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'd like to show the witness, please, what is now Exhibit P402. And if the binder for the witness could be given back to him so he can look at it in hard copy. And if we could call up on e-court page 31 in the English version and page 64 of the Macedonian version. And, Mr. Usher, if you could help the witness by turning to tab 1 of the Macedonian version and turning to page 64 of that version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Inspector, if you could take a look at the top of page 64 in the Macedonian version, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: For those following in English, we're at the bottom of page 31.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Inspector, do you see at the top of the page, there's a sentence beginning: "We must not allow for the terrorists to lead us to the negotiation table." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And this is from a statement that Minister Boskoski gave to journalists on the 6th of June, 2001. Inspector, if you look a little bit further down that paragraph -- excuse me, yeah, a little bit further down, you'll see a sentence that begins: "We must respond to terrorists." Do you see that, just a few lines down? Same paragraph where you were before: "We must respond to terrorists." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, if I could ask your assistance to direct the witness to the place in his language. You can take that, if you like. It's where the blue underline it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. That sentence reads the following: "We must respond to terrorists with the same manner and methods that they bring into play." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Inspector, does that sound like a call for revenge to you?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no comment to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, I'd like to ask you for a comment, please. I'd like you to answer my question.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Doesn't seem like revenge to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I see. All right. Inspector, prior to your testimony here in The Hague, did anyone ask you to say that you did not remember details about the events at Ljuboten in August 2001?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not correct. No one told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So you'll be pleased to know that that concludes the questions that will be asked of you. We thank you for your attendance in The Hague and the assistance you have given. You are now free to return to your other activities, and the court officer will show you out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution was informed yesterday that the Defence would require less time with this witness. Yesterday we made efforts to try to bring witnesses forward so the witness scheduled to testify on Friday will now be testifying tomorrow. We have also arranged to bring another ethnic Albanian crime base witness who was not previously scheduled to testify this week to The Hague. He will be arriving tomorrow and will be available to testify on Friday. We do not have another witness available at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That was the clear implication, Mr. Saxon. I think in the circumstances and due to the encouraging progress made with time, we must adjourn now to resume tomorrow at 2.15 in the hope that we will conclude these two witnesses on Thursday and Friday of this week. And I would ask the registry officer to explore with the technical people the continuing problems -- problem of background interference that we are receiving with the microphones. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 23rd day of August, 2007, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 3.35 p.m.,
